source.title: Quantifying Adaptability in Pre-trained Language Models with 500 Tasks
source.authors: Belinda Z. Li; Jane A. Yu; Madian Khabsa; Luke Zettlemoyer; A. Halevy; Jacob Andreas

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests memorization of randomly assigned word relations in a pretrained language model, a different task and model setting from random image labels.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own results on random word-relation tasks. These bear on V1's random-label fitting analogue. It does not test image inputs, corrupted-label fractions, shuffled or Gaussian inputs, explicit regularization, or learning real patterns before random labels.
record.test_reason: The study tests random-label memorization in a new setting: T5-base adapted to randomly assigned word outputs. Full fine-tuning reaches perfect training accuracy. Its comparisons of real and random task learning curves also bear on V6's learning-dynamics component.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the main memorization conclusion: full fine-tuning eventually perfectly memorizes random word associations, whereas prompt-tuning has substantially less memorization capacity. Its statement that random tasks are hardest needs restricting to the non-permuted experiments: Appendix E reports that random relations are easier than permuted lexical or factual relations under fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a pretrained T5-base adapted to synthetic word-relation tasks with fine-tuning or prompt-tuning, rather than training image classifiers from scratch on randomized image labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Adaptation paradigm changes memorization: fine-tuning eventually perfectly memorizes random relations; prompt-tuning is much less expressive and slower. Task type also changes convergence rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Under fine-tuning, random relations are learned faster than permuted lexical or factual relations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorization difficulty depends on whether arbitrary labels conflict with pretrained lexical or factual associations.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretraining accelerates memorization of novel permuted lexical and factual relations relative to a non-pretrained model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining provides an initialization that facilitates learning novel input-output mappings.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Evidence concerns one pretrained model family and synthetic word tasks rather than image classifiers. The text gives qualitative descriptions of the relevant curves, without exact final accuracies or numerical uncertainty for these comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows left out.

untested.parts: Chance-level test error, training from scratch in the main experiment, and whether randomization requires no hyperparameter changes. Hyperparameters were selected by trial and error; no controlled invariance test is reported.
A small constant-factor training-time increase relative to true labels and slowing with increasing corruption fraction. Qualitative task ordering supplies neither a time ratio nor a corruption sweep.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across increasing label-corruption fractions.
Controlled effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.

Learning shared signal before memorizing noise within the same partially corrupted training set. Separate-task comparisons do not establish this within-dataset sequence or distinguish new pattern learning from retrieval of pretrained knowledge.

missing.what: Comparative training curves showing lexical tasks learned first, factual tasks next, and random tasks last, separately for full fine-tuning and prompt-tuning.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text lacks readable numerical curves for Figures 2 and 6, so exact endpoint accuracies and real-versus-random convergence ratios cannot be recovered. Different input modality alone does not exclude V1, which is stated for standard deep networks rather than only image classifiers.

versions.untested_parts: Image classification, test error at chance, and whether the result holds across standard deep networks and without changes to their original architecture or hyperparameters.

rows.subject: pre-trained T5-base, fine-tuned
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on 1000 examples of random word associations; training-set memorization measured during adaptation.
rows.measure: Training-set accuracy on random word associations
rows.value: models can (eventually) learn to perfectly memorize ... entirely random word associations
rows.uncertainty: Shaded region shows standard error of the mean; numerical uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: Random word mappings are synthetic tasks, not random image labels; no numeric final accuracy or test error is given in the text.
rows.check: Perfect memorization is explicitly reported. The metric is per-token training accuracy, not exact-output accuracy. Chance-level test performance is not established numerically.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4; Section 5, Figure 2 and results paragraph; Appendix B.

rows.subject: pre-trained T5-base, prompt-tuned
rows.operation_detail: Prompt-tuned on 1000 examples of random word associations; training-set memorization measured during adaptation.
rows.measure: Training-set accuracy on random word associations
rows.value: takes over 200k updates to even begin performing nontrivially; none of the task types converge to 100% accuracy across tasks
rows.uncertainty: Shaded region shows standard error of the mean; numerical uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The text says prompt-tuning does not converge to 100% accuracy across tasks and is much less expressive; the update comparison is qualitative.
rows.check: Failure to reach perfect accuracy does not establish an absent effect: random-task performance eventually becomes nontrivial. This is restricted adaptation with the backbone frozen and only 100 new prompt embeddings trained. The approximately 20k versus over 200k update comparison concerns two adaptation methods on random tasks, not true versus random labels.

rows.subject: pre-trained T5-base, fine-tuned
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on permuted labels for atomic tasks; training-set memorization measured.

conditions.value: random relations versus permuted lexical or factual tasks

rows.measure: Relative ease of memorizing random labels
rows.value: random relations are easier to learn than permuted lexical or factual tasks
rows.note: The authors characterize permuted labels as unable to generalize; this is a comparison of synthetic task types, not image-label fitting.
rows.check: Relative learning speed across different randomized tasks does not establish zero training error or any version's real-versus-random comparison. The stated convergence-order reversal applies specifically to fine-tuning.

rows.subject: pre-trained T5-base, prompt-tuned
rows.operation_detail: Prompt-tuned on permuted labels for atomic tasks; training-set memorization measured.

conditions.value: pre-trained versus non-pre-trained model; random relations versus permuted lexical or factual tasks

rows.measure: Relative ease of memorizing novel or random labels
rows.baseline: non-pretrained model on permuted tasks; pre-trained model on permuted lexical or factual tasks
rows.value: pre-trained models can memorize novel word relations faster than non-pre-trained models; random relations are easier to learn than permuted lexical or factual tasks
rows.note: Qualitative comparisons only; no numeric learning-time values are provided in the text.
rows.check: Combines distinct comparisons that should be separated. Faster memorization with pretraining does not establish perfect fitting. The statement that random relations are easier than permuted lexical or factual tasks is explicitly made for fine-tuning, so its attribution to prompt-tuning is unsupported.
